title: Other precision weighting mechanisms
excerpt: Neuromodulators provide a powerful global and state-dependent handle on gain, but they are only one layer of the precision-control stack; the cortex also implements precision weighting through several other mechanisms: Apical dendritic gating: compartment-leve
html:
Neuromodulators provide a powerful global and state-dependent handle on gain, but they are only one layer of the precision-control stack; the cortex also implements precision weighting through several other mechanisms: The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Apical dendritic gating: compartment-level precision switching. The finest-grained precision control can occur at the single-neuron level via the functional compartmentalization of pyramidal dendritic trees. Driving sensory/feedforward inputs tend to impinge more strongly on basal dendrites and perisomatic circuits, whereas cortico-cortical feedback/contextual signals are especially enriched in layer 1 and preferentially target the apical tuft–a segregation that provides a natural substrate for differentially reweighting evidence-dominated vs context/prior-dominated influences in hierarchical predictive architectures. Rather than acting as a separate "error computer," the apical compartment can be viewed as a gain-control channel whose effective influence on somatic output spans a wide dynamic range: when apical depolarization is weak, its impact on spike output is often modest and primarily modulatory; when sufficiently strong apical drive coincides with basal drive and backpropagating activity, regenerative dendritic events (e.g., BAC firing via apical Ca2+^{2+} electrogenesis) can supralinearly amplify somatic output, effectively increasing the leverage of feedback/context on the neuron’s response 1, 2. This amplification is, however, not an all-or-none "precision bit": the probability, timing, and amplitude of apical Ca2+^{2+} events vary continuously with the balance of apical excitation, basal drive, dendritic nonlinearities, and inhibition, yielding a graded control of how strongly apical information shapes output. This apical gain is strongly regulated by dendrite-targeting inhibition, including SST+^{+} Martinotti cells that innervate the apical tuft and can raise the threshold for (or suppress) apical regenerative events; conversely, VIP→\rightarrowSST disinhibition can release this brake, biasing the circuit toward greater apical influence and thereby providing a pathway by which behavioral state and neuromodulatory context can tune feedback efficacy at the dendritic level 3. Disruption of apical integration (for example, via NMDA hypofunction and impaired dendritic nonlinearities) has been proposed as a precision-control failure contributing to core cognitive deficits in schizophrenia 4. For learning, apical Ca2+^{2+} spikes can also gate and shape plasticity by generating large, prolonged dendritic calcium transients that bias the induction of LTP/LTD at co-active feedforward synapses, coupling precision-weighted inference with precision-weighted learning at the level of single cells (also covered in "Cortical Plasticity") 1, 2. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Oscillatory synchrony: temporal windowing of error propagation. Neural oscillations provide an intermediate-timescale control channel for effective connectivity, adjusting cycle by cycle which populations can influence one another. In the communication-through-coherence (CTC) framework, inter-areal transmission is most effective when sender and receiver rhythms are phase-aligned such that presynaptic spikes arrive during high-excitability phases of the receiver; misalignment reduces the postsynaptic impact of the same spike trains 5, 6. Coherence can therefore be treated as a temporal gate on pathway gain (and, in predictive-coding terms, can be interpreted as scaling the effective precision of signals along that pathway), although an important alternative view is that some forms of coherence may arise as a consequence of communication rather than its cause 7. A large body of work supports a spectral asymmetry in cortical routing: feedforward-directed influences are often strongest in higher-frequency bands (gamma, and in some analyses theta/gamma), whereas feedback-directed influences are strongest in lower-frequency bands (alpha/beta) 8, 9, 10. Consistent with this, attention increases gamma-band synchronization/coherence between lower and higher visual areas, strengthening effective feedforward drive 10. Conversely, increased alpha power over task-irrelevant/unattended regions predicts worse perceptual performance and is well modeled as rhythmic inhibitory pulsing that reduces local excitability and sensory throughput 11. This "gamma-up / alpha-down (or alpha-up in suppressed regions)" pattern naturally supports spectral multiplexing: ascending error-like signals and descending context/prediction-like signals can be differentially gated–even along the same anatomical pathways–by shifting coherence and power in the corresponding bands 6, 12. Theta-range rhythms (~4-8 Hz) further organize processing over longer windows, and theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling can nest fast, high-gain processing epochs inside slower control cycles 13. These oscillatory gates interact with slower precision channels: neuromodulators can bias the global oscillatory regime (e.g., cholinergic engagement often promotes gamma and theta-gamma coupling and reshapes low-frequency rhythms in a task- and region-dependent manner); the net result is a multi-scale temporal precision architecture in which neuromodulators set the slow envelope and oscillatory synchrony supplies rapid, cycle-by-cycle gating 13, 11, 6. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Population variability as intrinsic gain control. Trial-to-trial variability in neural population responses is not merely a nuisance that obscures a separately computed precision signal–it directly implements precision weighting through its effect on gain. When shared variability is high (elevated Fano factors, strong low-dimensional noise correlations), the population’s net drive to downstream targets is inconsistent across repetitions: the same nominal prediction error produces a noisy, temporally smeared volley whose postsynaptic impact is effectively attenuated by the incoherence of its constituent spikes. A high-variance error representation is, by simple biophysics, a low-gain error representation–and therefore a low-precision one. Conversely, stimulus onset, attention, and confident perceptual states are all associated with a suppression of shared variability 14, 15, 16, 17, which tightens the population response around its mean, increases the reliability and temporal coherence of the output volley, and thereby raises the effective gain with which that population’s prediction errors influence downstream inference and plasticity. In this view, precision need not be represented as a separate scalar quantity and then multiplicatively applied to error units; rather, the statistical structure of the error-coding population itself determines how heavily that error is weighted in the global loss. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Thalamocortical precision gating. Every cortical area participates in reciprocal thalamocortical loops, and a growing body of work supports the view that thalamus is not a passive relay but a reconfigurable gain/routing node that helps determine which signals are amplified and broadcast to and between cortical areas–and when. The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN)–a GABAergic shell that receives excitatory collaterals from both corticothalamic (especially L6) projections and thalamocortical relay axons–projects inhibition back onto thalamic relay neurons, providing a circuit substrate for state- and context-dependent inhibitory gating that can act like gain control over thalamocortical throughput (often approximating divisive effects depending on operating point and network state) 18, 19. Consistent with an attentional "mask" implemented upstream of cortex, TRN activity can decrease for attended stimuli (disinhibiting relay) and increase when attention is directed elsewhere, shaping relay responses early in the sensory stream and plausibly contributing to cross-channel suppression before cortical attentional effects fully emerge 20. Beyond first-order relays, higher-order thalamic nuclei (e.g., pulvinar, mediodorsal nucleus) receive driver-like input from cortical L5 and return projections to superficial layers across multiple cortical areas, creating transthalamic corticocortical pathways that can regulate directed inter-areal communication rather than merely retransmitting peripheral input 21, 19. In the visual system, the pulvinar has been shown to coordinate attention-dependent inter-areal coupling–particularly in the alpha band–such that pulvinar activity is consistent with a coordinating (and not purely reflective) role in shaping cortical synchrony and effective connectivity across visual areas 22, 23. Within predictive-coding/active-inference framings, this naturally invites an interpretation in which higher-order thalamus helps set the effective precision/gain of inter-areal message passing (e.g., amplifying attended channels and down-weighting unattended ones via corticothalamic control of transthalamic gain) 24. These thalamic precision/routing mechanisms dovetail with other gain channels: cholinergic input can depolarize many relay neurons and exerts receptor-specific (nicotinic/muscarinic) control over TRN excitability, reshaping TRN-mediated inhibition and thus relay throughput; noradrenergic input from locus coeruleus tends to bias relay neurons toward tonic, relay-competent firing and reduce rhythmic bursting, altering both linear fidelity and salience sensitivity 21, 19. More generally, thalamocortical loops are deeply intertwined with cortical oscillatory regimes (including alpha/beta generators and state-dependent synchrony), making thalamus a plausible convergence point where neuromodulatory state, oscillatory coordination, and feedback control jointly determine which signals enter cortex and which inter-areal channels dominate moment-to-moment computation 19, 22, 23. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The five precision-weighting mechanisms operate at different spatial scales (single dendritic compartments local populations inter-areal thalamic routing brain-wide modulatory broadcasts), different temporal scales (single oscillatory cycles at 1̃0-25 ms neuromodulatory state changes over seconds), and on different aspects of the precision tensor (compartment-specific gating, mean gain, temporal windowing, covariance structure, inter-areal routing). Their joint action implements the full Πl\Pi_l field: neuromodulators set the slow, state-dependent envelope; the thalamus gates which inter-areal channels are open; oscillatory coherence provides cycle-by-cycle temporal gating; apical dendritic mechanisms control compartment-level prior-likelihood integration; and population variability quenching reflects the aggregate precision achieved by the ensemble. The result is a deeply layered precision architecture that allows the cortex to continuously reshape its effective loss function in response to attention, arousal, uncertainty, and task demands, without altering the synaptic weights that define the generative model itself. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).
